nameStory: Brazilian watermeal gets its name from its tiny, grain-like appearance that resembles miniature meal or flour scattered on the water's surface. The "Brazilian" part refers to its South American origins, though this little floating plant has made itself at home throughout the Americas.
description: Brazilian watermeal is one of the world's smallest flowering plants, so tiny you might mistake it for green specks of dust floating on pond water. Each individual plant is just a tiny green oval, smaller than a pinhead, with no leaves, stems, or roots whatsoever. These miniature plants form dense floating mats on the surface of calm ponds and slow-moving water, creating what looks like a green carpet or scum.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Incredibly tiny - each plant is only about 1 millimeter long, roughly the size of a grain of coarse sand or small crumb

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Flat, oval-shaped green body with a small bump or raised area in the center, like a tiny green coin with a dimple

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense floating mats on water surfaces that feel slightly slimy when you run your fingers through them

idTips.label: Plant Structure
idTips.description: Completely lacks any leaves, stems, or roots - just a simple green floating body

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to medium green, sometimes appearing yellowish-green in dense colonies

habitat: Look for Brazilian watermeal floating on the surface of calm, still waters like ponds, slow streams, and quiet backwaters. It prefers nutrient-rich water and is often found in the same spots where you'd see duckweed, though it's much smaller.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water warms, though individual plants are so small they're easily overlooked among other aquatic vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when dense mats are most visible and easiest to spot floating on warm pond surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Colonies may persist into early fall but become less noticeable as growth slows with cooler temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Plants typically die back or become dormant, surviving as tiny dormant buds that will regrow the following spring.

funFact: Brazilian watermeal holds the world record as the smallest flowering plant on Earth - you could fit about 5,000 of them on a single penny, yet each tiny speck is capable of producing even tinier flowers and seeds!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with algae or pond scum, but unlike algae, watermeal consists of individual tiny plants rather than stringy or slimy masses. Memory trick: if you can see individual tiny green specks (with a magnifying glass), it's probably watermeal; if it's just green slime, it's likely algae.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Brazilian," this species is native throughout much of North and South America. The extreme rarity of observations in New England (only 6 recorded) suggests it may be at the northern edge of its range or easily overlooked due to its microscopic size.
compareHints: Brazilian watermeal is virtually identical to its relatives Columbian watermeal and dotted watermeal, and they can only be reliably distinguished under a microscope by examining flower structure and surface texture details. In the field, all three species of watermeal look like tiny floating green specks and are much smaller than the more familiar duckweeds, which have distinct leaf-like structures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Columbian watermeal is nearly identical to other watermeal species and requires microscopic examination to distinguish definitively.
Dotted watermeal is distinguished from its watermeal relatives by those characteristic tiny dots or punctures on its surface that give it its name.
